response.vignette:
A 32-year-old woman was brought by her husband with a 6-month history of increasingly erratic behavior. Over the preceding 4 months she had slept 2–3 hours per night, lost 15 kg, and experienced palpitations. She reported racing thoughts, long hours of unproductive work, and intermittent paranoid ideas, including believing that her mobile telephone was sending messages directly into her brain. She had worsening anxiety, difficulty caring for her child, and episodes of wandering behavior. She was previously healthy, took no medications, and had no family history of thyroid disease.

In the emergency department she was easily distracted, made intermittent eye contact, paced the room, and had pressured speech without hallucinations or intent to self-harm; her paranoid ideas were not held with delusional intensity. Routine laboratory tests revealed a suppressed TSH level (<0.01 mU/L), an elevated free thyroxine level (97.5 pmol/L), and an elevated free triiodothyronine level (32.3 pmol/L). Other blood tests, including full blood count, C-reactive protein, electrolytes, and liver function tests, were normal. 

Her vital signs showed a temperature of 36.7 °C, heart rate of 120 beats/min, blood pressure of 162/85 mm Hg, and respiratory rate of 23 breaths/min. On physical examination she had a visible, smooth, non-tender goitre and lid lag but no tremor, ophthalmopathy, dermopathy, or other skin changes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
